The Messy Fight Over California’s Proposed Billionaire Tax Divides Democrats
 
Plus, shoppers are convinced businesses are using AI to charge higher prices, and more U.S. manufacturing jobs require a college degree
 
 
JAE C. HONG/AP
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

The idea seemed simple at first: a one-time tax on California’s billionaires to counter looming cuts to Medicaid.

 

Instead, the proposed wealth tax has exposed deep divisions among Democrats and created strange bedfellows on both sides working to defeat or pass the proposal.

 

Drama surrounding the measure includes a fight among labor unions worried their own priorities will suffer, tech elites putting down hundreds of millions to defeat it, and allegations of extortion and harassment by the tax’s architect.

 

The messy fight has gripped California for the past year and shows how enacting a long-heralded concept on the left—taxing billionaires’ stratospheric wealth—is far from easy, even in one of the nation’s bluest states, Laura J. Nelson and Paul Kiernan explain.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva achieved a surprise victory over Flávio Bolsonaro, winning an unprecedented fourth term as president.

 

• Fed officials’ calls for patience and the approaching midterms make a surprise rate increase this week hard to pull off, even after firmer inflation readings. These are the 19 people in the room when the Fed sets rates.

 

• France, working with European allies, is strengthening and expanding its role as a nuclear-weapons power in an effort to bolster deterrence against Russian attacks as Europe’s confidence in American security guarantees wavers. 

 

• A former Russian energy industry insider has sued sanctioned oil traders who, according to Western officials, have become the most important middlemen enabling Moscow to sell its oil and fund its war in Ukraine.

• Big investors are piling into a barely known commercial real-estate business—industrial outdoor storage—seizing on demand from data-center developers.

 

• Siemens Energy is outselling GE Vernova on gas turbines. The German energy giant is an overlooked bargain, writes Jinjoo Lee.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Why so many shoppers think retailers are using AI to jack up prices.

 

Nick Nadeau recently bought a hard drive through Walmart’s app—and got a bad feeling about its price. On Nadeau’s phone, Walmart listed the drive for $369. On his wife’s phone, however, the drive cost $110 less. American shoppers are convinced that businesses are deploying technology to charge more, using AI to quickly change prices by assessing their needs or profile. A spokeswoman for Walmart said the hard drive prices varied because of an error that has been corrected, not because it used personal information to calibrate the price of a product. Such denials have failed to stanch the concerns of shoppers and consumer activists, Sarah Nassauer reports.

 

5.

 

U.S. manufacturing is adding jobs again. You might need a college degree to get one.

 

Swift Coat, a maker of antireflective coated glass for satellites, plans to hire two or three workers by the end of the year at its facility in northern Phoenix. All positions will require an engineering degree. Swift is part of a broader shift in America’s factory landscape, reports Konrad Putzier. U.S. manufacturers have increased their head count by 72,000 since December, after years of declining employment. But these aren’t your grandfather’s factory jobs. Manufacturers are hiring more white-collar workers in management and business operations. And blue-collar roles increasingly require advanced training as factories become more automated and complex.

 
 
 

Ask us your questions about midterms and the economy.
What do you want to know about how the economy will influence midterm voters across the country? Our reporters Eliza Collins and Konrad Putzier will answer your queries in the comments space from 1-2 p.m. ET tomorrow. Ask your questions for them now.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

What we saw on the ground at seven Trump rallies in seven days.

 
 
KENT NISHIMURA/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

Journal reporters attended every one of President Trump’s midterm rallies in the past week, starting in Kansas on Monday and ending in Michigan on Sunday, with stops along the way in North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, Florida and Georgia. On stage, the president is met with cheering crowds and fleeting signs of opposition. Crowds are generally smaller than they were when he was on the ballot, but Trump is reveling in the attention, touting his agenda, stirring the pot and veering off script.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING TODAY

8. THE NUMBER

 
7 days
 

That’s how long New York City delays clearing homeless encampments under a policy implemented by Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration. The extra time gives outreach workers an opportunity to persuade people to accept services and offer them a chance to secure their belongings. Residents and businesses say the approach allows individuals to, in effect, evade removal by telegraphing that if they relocate across the street on the sixth day then the seven-day clock will restart.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

The dangers and delights of recording audio for the steamiest books around.

 

With no movie or streaming adaptations for the hit Sarah J. Maas series “A Court of Thorns and Roses,” full-cast audio versions of the novels play an outsize role. The cast members have become niche celebrities across romantasy, the literary genre blending romance and fantasy. But it comes with dangers. For readers who’ve heard these characters differently in their heads—including fans around the world who can’t believe how American everyone sounds—it’s open season.
